mathgap.title: Signed 'has N more than'
mathgap.principle: When a statement says 'X has N more than Y', interpret it as the signed equation X = Y + N. Do not invert the relationship or treat it as Y = X + N.
mathgap.when_to_apply: Whenever you encounter a direct statement of the form 'X has N more than Y'.
mathgap.example: Interpreting 'X has N more than Y' as Y = X + N instead of X = Y + N.

mathgap.title: Signed relational equation
mathgap.principle: For statements like 'The number of X that A has more than B is equal to the difference between the number of X that C and D have', translate directly to (A - B) = (C - D), preserving the order of subtraction on both sides. Do not use absolute values.
mathgap.when_to_apply: When a relational equation involves a 'has more than' clause together with a 'difference between' clause.
mathgap.example: Treating the equation as |A - B| = |C - D| instead of (A - B) = (C - D).

mathgap.title: Signed 'difference between'
mathgap.principle: The phrase 'difference between the number of X that C and D have' means the signed subtraction C - D in the order presented, not the absolute difference.
mathgap.when_to_apply: Whenever a statement mentions the 'difference between' two persons' counts.
mathgap.example: Using |C - D| instead of (C - D) for the right‑hand side of a relational equation.

mathgap.title: Allow negative differences
mathgap.principle: Do not assume that a 'has more than' clause guarantees a positive difference; the equation may legitimately yield a negative value, which should be kept as‑is for solving the system.
mathgap.when_to_apply: When a 'has more than' equation seems contradictory or produces a negative left‑hand side.
mathgap.example: Discarding a solution because A - B is negative, assuming A must be larger than B.

mathgap.title: Model transfers as net changes
mathgap.principle: Each statement 'X gives N to Y' reduces X's count by N and increases Y's count by N. Apply all such transfers after establishing the initial amounts.
mathgap.when_to_apply: Whenever a transfer of items is described.
mathgap.example: Adding N to the giver's count instead of subtracting it.

mathgap.title: Initial count statements
mathgap.principle: Plain statements like 'X has N' describe the initial amount before any transfers. Use them as starting values and adjust later with transfers.
mathgap.when_to_apply: When encountering a simple 'has N' statement without any transfer verb.
mathgap.example: Treating 'X has N' as the final amount after all transfers.

mathgap.title: Systematic equation solving
mathgap.principle: Represent each person as a variable, write a linear equation for every relational statement and every transfer, then solve the resulting linear system using substitution or elimination.
mathgap.when_to_apply: When the problem contains many interdependent statements.
mathgap.example: Guessing individual values without forming a system of equations.

mathgap.title: Handle contradictory 'more than' statements
mathgap.principle: If two statements appear to contradict (e.g., A has more than B and B has more than A), keep both as signed equations. The system may still be solvable; the wording may be imprecise.
mathgap.when_to_apply: When encountering seemingly contradictory relational statements.
mathgap.example: Abandoning the problem because of contradictory 'has more than' clauses.

mathgap.title: Order of applying transfers
mathgap.principle: The final net result of multiple transfers is independent of the order in which they are applied; you can apply them in any sequence after setting the initial counts.
mathgap.when_to_apply: When several transfers involve the same individuals and the order is unclear.
mathgap.example: Applying a transfer before the giver's initial count has been established.

mathgap.title: Distinct variables for similar names
mathgap.principle: Treat each distinct name as a separate variable, even if the names are similar (e.g., Orval vs Orville). Do not merge them unless the problem explicitly states they refer to the same person.
mathgap.when_to_apply: When the problem includes names that differ by only a few letters.
mathgap.example: Combining Orval and Orville into a single variable.

mathgap.description: Using absolute value for 'difference between' clauses
mathgap.why_it_happens: The word 'difference' is often interpreted colloquially as an absolute distance, leading to |A‑B| instead of the signed subtraction A‑B.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: Remember that in these puzzles 'difference between' means the signed subtraction in the order presented: treat it as (A - B).

mathgap.description: Assuming positivity for 'has more than' statements
mathgap.why_it_happens: Natural‑language intuition suggests the left side should be larger, causing solvers to discard equations that yield a negative difference.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: Write the equation exactly as stated (A - B = …) and accept negative values; the puzzle may use the wording loosely.

mathgap.description: Treating 'X has N' as a final count after transfers
mathgap.why_it_happens: Uncertainty about whether the given counts are before or after the described transfers leads to using them as final values.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: Assume such statements describe the initial state; apply all transfers afterwards to obtain final counts.

mathgap.description: Applying transfers in the wrong direction
mathgap.why_it_happens: Misreading the verb 'gives' can cause the solver to add to the giver instead of subtracting.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: Remember that 'X gives N to Y' means X loses N and Y gains N; update both counts accordingly.

mathgap.why_it_happens: Seeing two statements that appear to conflict can make the solver think the system is unsolvable and abandon systematic solving.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: Keep both equations as signed relations; the overall system may still have a unique solution despite apparent contradictions.
